ABSTRACT


The

objective

of

this

study

is

to

understand

collectivity

within

the

Landless

Rural

Workers’

Movement

(MST)

in

the

region

of

the

former

Annoni

Farm

and,

based

on

this

experience,

to

discuss

and

(re)think

Collective

Health.

It

starts

from

the

understanding

of

the

importance

and

necessity

of

collectivity

both

in

the

historical

and

current

constitution

of

the

MST

and

in

the

Brazilian

Health

Reform

Movement,

as

well

as

in

what

follows

from

Collective

Health.

The

methodological

approach

is

grounded

in

qualitative

research

of

ethnographic

inspiration,

with

field

insertions

in

the

settlement

region

of

the

former

Annoni

Farm,

in

the

northern

region

of

Rio

Grande

do

Sul,

as

well

as

other

engagements

with

the

MST

made

possible

by

the

methodological

paths

and

by

being

in

the

field.

Through

participant

observation

with

the

Landless

in

communities,

homes,

cooperatives,

meetings,

occupations,

and

educational

institutions,

it

was

possible

to

experience

collectivity

in

its

everyday

materiality,

considering

struggles,

histories,

and

contradictions.

Conversations,

interviews,

photographs,

documentary

research,

and

the

construction

of

field

diaries

were

carried

out.

The

results

and

discussion

are

presented

in

four

chapters:

the

first

presents

encounters

with

the

research

field

and

the

ensuing

possibilities

for

discussion;

the

second

highlights

the

importance

of

memory

of

struggles,

references,

and

symbols

for

the

everyday

maintenance

of

collectivity;

the

third

presents

organicity

as

a

strategy

and

possible

practice

of

collective

organization,

sharing

of

responsibilities,

and

preservation

of

cadres

and

common

ideals;

the

fourth

seeks

to

elucidate

educational

and

work

practices

that

materialize

collectivity.

The

discussion

of

the

findings,

based

on

experiences

within

the

MST

in

dialogue

with

Collective

Health,

highlights

contrasts

between

conceptions

of

collectivity,

especially

when

compared

to

those

rooted

in

the

historical

construction

of

social

movements,

in

organicity,

strategy

and

concession,

in

grassroots

work

and

cadre

renewal,

in

the

working

class

and

the

people,

and

in

the

ongoing

tension

driven

by

the

advance

of

capital.

In

addition

to

its

originality

in

exploring

connections

about

collectivity

between

Collective

Health

and

the

MST,

its

applicability

to

the

field

of

Collective

Health

lies

in

the

resumption

of

studies

that

seek

to

understand

and

rethink

collectivity

within

its

scope.

Thus,

values

and

principles

that

are

daily

erased

in

health

service

practices

by

the

capitalist

mode

of

production

–

which

dominates

the

economic

and

productive

complex

of

health

–

are

reaffirmed,

distorting

the

republican

aim

of

building

a

health

system

for

and

with

the

people,

where

all

understand

themselves

as

part

of

the

people.

The

final

considerations

reflect

on

confronting

the

limits

of

an

incomplete

health

reform.

The

approximation

with

the

MST

points

to

the

understanding

that

collectivity

is

not

produced

spontaneously,

requiring

political

intentionality,

organization,

and

material

and

symbolic

conditions

for

its

sustenance.

Thus,

this

study

aims

to

provoke

a

revisiting

of

the

foundations

of

Collective

Health

so

that

the

social,

the

collective,

and

class

consciousness

may

become

central

to

reflections

on

work,

education,

and

care

in

health.

ABSTRACT


The

objective

of

this

study

is

to

understand

within

Rural

Workers’

Movement

(MST)

in

the

region

of

the

former

Annoni

Farm

and,

based

on

this

experience,

to

discuss

and

(re)think

Collective

Health.

It

starts

from

the

understanding

of

the

importance

and

necessity

of

collectivity

both

in

the

historical

and

current

constitution

of

the

MST

and

in

the

Brazilian

Health

Reform

Movement,

as

well

as

in

what

follows

from

Collective

Health.

The

methodological

approach

is

grounded

in

qualitative

research

of

ethnographic

inspiration,

with

field

insertions

in

the

settlement

region

of

the

former

Annoni

Farm,

in

the

northern

region

of

Rio

Grande

do

Sul,

as

well

as

other

engagements

with

the

MST

made

possible

by

the

methodological

paths

and

by

being

in

the

field.

Through

participant

observation

with

the

Landless

in

communities,

homes,

cooperatives,

meetings,

occupations,

and

educational

institutions,

it

was

possible

to

experience

collectivity

in

its

everyday

materiality,

considering

struggles,

histories,

and

contradictions.

Conversations,

interviews,

photographs,

documentary

research,

and

the

construction

of

field

diaries

were

carried

out.

The

results

and

discussion

are

presented

in

four

chapters:

the

first

presents

encounters

with

the

research

field

and

the

ensuing

possibilities

for

discussion;

the

second

highlights

the

importance

of

memory

of

struggles,

references,

and

symbols

for

the

everyday

maintenance

of

collectivity;

the

third

presents

organicity

as

a

strategy

and

possible

practice

of

collective

organization,

sharing

of

responsibilities,

and

preservation

of

cadres

and

common

ideals;

the

fourth

seeks

to

elucidate

educational

and

work

practices

that

materialize

collectivity.

The

discussion

of

the

findings,

based

on

experiences

within

the

MST

in

dialogue

with

Collective

Health,

highlights

contrasts

between

conceptions

of

collectivity,

especially

when

compared

to

those

rooted

in

the

historical

construction

of

social

movements,

in

organicity,

strategy

and

concession,

in

grassroots

work

and

cadre

renewal,

in

the

working

class

and

the

people,

and

in

the

ongoing

tension

driven

by

the

advance

of

capital.

In

addition

to

its

originality

in

exploring

connections

about

collectivity

between

Collective

Health

and

the

MST,

its

applicability

to

the

field

of

Collective

Health

lies

in

the

resumption

of

studies

that

seek

to

understand

and

rethink

collectivity

within

its

scope.

Thus,

values

and

principles

that

are

daily

erased

in

health

service

practices

by

the

capitalist

mode

of

production

–

which

dominates

the

economic

and

productive

complex

of

health

distorting

the

republican

aim

health

with

people,

all

understand

part

an

incomplete
